summary.text: Writing \(p=2m+1\), Lucas congruences split each sum for \(p+d\) (\(0\le d<p-1\)) into vanishing middle terms and cancelling \(k,p+k\) tails, while \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives \(a(p-1)\equiv1\) and divisibility of central binomial coefficients leaves only \(k=m\) in \(c(p-1)\), giving \((-1)^m\). Thus both Hankel matrices are zero beyond the anti-diagonal, so only the reversing permutation contributes to each determinant; its sign is \((-1)^m\), yielding the first value directly and cancelling the product of the second matrix’s constant anti-diagonal entries to give \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                       \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad p=2m+1.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\), or equivalently identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first collect the binomial congruences that will be used.

For \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(k>0\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k,
\]
and \(k!\) is invertible modulo \(p\). The case \(k=0\) is immediate.

We will also use the following one-step form of Lucas's congruence. For arbitrary nonnegative integers \(N,K\),
\[
\binom NK\equiv
 \binom{N\bmod p}{K\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{\lfloor K/p\rfloor}. \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, write \(N=N_0+pN_1\) and \(K=K_0+pK_1\), where \(0\le N_0,K_0<p\). In \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), the freshman's-dream identity gives
\[
(1+x)^N=(1+x)^{N_0}\bigl((1+x)^p\bigr)^{N_1}
       =(1+x)^{N_0}(1+x^p)^{N_1}.
\]
In the product on the right, a monomial of degree \(K_0+pK_1\) can only arise by taking degree \(K_0\) from the first factor and degree \(pK_1\) from the second: the degree chosen from the first factor is less than \(p\) and hence is determined by its residue modulo \(p\). Comparing coefficients proves (2), with the convention that \(\binom uv=0\) for \(v>u\).

Several consequences will be needed. If \(0\le d<p\), then for \(0\le j<p\),
\[
\binom{p+d}{p+j}\equiv\binom dj, \tag{3}
\]
and for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv\binom dk. \tag{4}
\]
In particular, the latter is zero when \(d<k<p\). These statements follow at once from (2), because the base-\(p\) digits of \(p+d\) are \((1,d)\), while those of \(p+j\) are \((1,j)\) and those of \(k\) are \((0,k)\).

Let
\[
B(r)=\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
If \(0\le r<p\) and \(p\le2r\), then
\[
B(r)\equiv0. \tag{5}
\]
One direct explanation is that \(r<p\) and \(2r<2p\), so \((2r)!\) contains exactly one factor of \(p\), whereas neither copy of \(r!\) contains a factor of \(p\). Thus \(p\mid (2r)!/(r!)^2\).

We also need, for every \(0\le r<p\),
\[
B(p+r)=\binom{2p+2r}{p+r}\equiv2B(r). \tag{6}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2r<p\), applying (2) to the top number with base-\(p\) digits \((2,2r)\) and the bottom number with digits \((1,r)\) gives
\[
\binom{2p+2r}{p+r}\equiv\binom21\binom{2r}{r}=2B(r).
\]
If \(2r\ge p\), then (5) says that \(B(r)\equiv0\). On the left, the low base-\(p\) digits are \(2r-p\) and \(r\). Since \(r<p\), one has \(2r-p<r\), and therefore the low-digit binomial coefficient \(\binom{2r-p}{r}\) is zero. Thus both sides of (6) are zero.

We now evaluate the two sequences at \(p-1\).

Using (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(p=2m+1\) terms in this alternating sum, so all adjacent pairs cancel and one term remains. Hence
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1. \tag{7}
\]

For \(c(p-1)\), consider a summand indexed by \(k\), where \(0\le k<p\). If \(k<m\), then
\[
r=p-1-k=2m-k
\]
satisfies \(r<p\) and \(2r\ge p\), so (5) gives
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=B(r)\equiv0.
\]
If \(k>m\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so \(B(k)\equiv0\). Consequently every summand vanishes except the one with \(k=m\). At that index, \(p-1=2m\) and \(p-1-m=m\), so all three binomial quantities appearing in the summand are \(\binom{2m}{m}=\binom{p-1}{m}\), with the first one squared. By (1), this common binomial coefficient is congruent to \((-1)^m\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2B(m)^2\\
&\equiv (-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^4
 =(-1)^m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}. \tag{8}
\]

The next essential fact is that both sequences vanish modulo \(p\) throughout the range needed below:
\[
a(p+d)\equiv c(p+d)\equiv0
\qquad(0\le d<p-1). \tag{9}
\]
We prove the two assertions separately.

Set \(n=p+d\). For \(a(n)\), split its defining sum into the three index ranges
\[
0\le k\le d,\qquad d<k<p,\qquad p\le k\le p+d.
\]
For \(d<k<p\), equation (4) gives \(\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv\binom dk=0\), so every middle summand vanishes.

The last range can be written \(k=p+j\), with \(0\le j\le d\). Equations (3) and (4) give
\[
\binom{p+d}{p+j}\equiv\binom dj
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{p+d}{j}\equiv\binom dj.
\]
Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+j}=-(-1)^j.
\]
It follows that the summand at \(p+j\) is the negative of the summand at \(j\):
\[
(-1)^{p+j}\binom{p+d}{p+j}^4
\equiv-(-1)^j\binom{p+d}{j}^4.
\]
The first and last ranges therefore cancel term by term. This proves \(a(p+d)\equiv0\).

For \(c(n)\), write its \(k\)-th summand as
\[
T_n(k)=(-1)^k\binom nk^2 B(k)B(n-k).
\]
Again, every term with \(d<k<p\) vanishes by (4), because \(\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv0\).

It remains to pair \(T_n(j)\) with \(T_n(p+j)\) for \(0\le j\le d\). We have
\[
\binom{p+d}{p+j}\equiv\binom dj
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{p+d}{j}\equiv\binom dj.
\]
Moreover, by (6),
\[
B(p+j)\equiv2B(j).
\]
Since \(n-(p+j)=d-j\), this gives
\[
T_n(p+j)
\equiv -(-1)^j\binom dj^2\,2B(j)B(d-j). \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, \(n-j=p+(d-j)\), and \(0\le d-j<p\). Another use of (6) yields
\[
B(n-j)=B(p+d-j)\equiv2B(d-j).
\]
Consequently
\[
T_n(j)
\equiv (-1)^j\binom dj^2\,B(j)\,2B(d-j), \tag{11}
\]
which is the negative of (10). Thus all remaining terms cancel in pairs, proving \(c(p+d)\equiv0\). This establishes (9).

Now form the two \(p\times p\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_p\)
\[
\overline A_{ij}=a(i+j),
\qquad
\overline C_{ij}=c(i+j),
\qquad 0\le i,j<p,
\]
where the integer entries are reduced modulo \(p\). If \(i+j\ge p\), put \(d=i+j-p\). Since \(i,j\le p-1\),
\[
0\le d\le p-2<p-1.
\]
Equation (9) therefore shows that
\[
\overline A_{ij}=\overline C_{ij}=0
\qquad\text{whenever }i+j\ge p. \tag{12}
\]
Thus both matrices are zero strictly beyond their reverse diagonal.

We record the determinant consequence of this shape. Suppose \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) is any matrix over a commutative ring such that \(M_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i+j\ge p\). Let
\[
\rho(j)=p-1-j
\]
be the reversal permutation. In the determinant expansion
\[
\det M=\sum_{\tau\in S_p}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)
                    \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}M_{\tau(j),j},
\]
the only potentially nonzero term is the term belonging to \(\rho\).

Indeed, if the product belonging to \(\tau\) is nonzero, then for every \(j\) one must have
\[
\tau(j)+j\le p-1,
\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad
\tau(j)\le p-1-j. \tag{13}
\]
Summing (13) over all \(j\), the left side is
\(
\sum_j\tau(j)=\sum_jj
\)
because \(\tau\) is a permutation. The sum of the right sides is also
\(
\sum_j(p-1-j)=\sum_jj.
\)
Thus equality must hold in every inequality in (13); if one were strict, the sum would be strict. Hence \(\tau(j)=p-1-j\) for all \(j\), so \(\tau=\rho\). It follows that
\[
\det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
       \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}M_{p-1-j,j}. \tag{14}
\]

The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct positions in increasing order, so
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^{\binom p2}
=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=m(2m+1),
\]
whose parity is the parity of \(m\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^m
=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}. \tag{15}
\]

Apply (14) first to \(\overline A\). Every reverse-diagonal entry has index sum \(p-1\), and hence by (7)
\[
\overline A_{p-1-j,j}=a(p-1)\equiv1.
\]
Using (15),
\[
\det\overline A
=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}1
=(-1)^m.
\]
Reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with the determinant, since the determinant is an integer polynomial in the matrix entries. Thus, for the original integer matrix
\(A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\),
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^m=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Finally apply (14) to \(\overline C\). By (8), every reverse-diagonal entry is \((-1)^m\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det\overline C
&=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
  \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}(-1)^m\\
&=(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p
 =(-1)^{m(p+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
But \(p+1=2m+2=2(m+1)\), so
\[
m(p+1)=2m(m+1)
\]
is even. Therefore \(\det\overline C=1\). Again commuting determinant with reduction modulo \(p\), for the integer matrix
\(C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\) we obtain
\[
\det C\equiv1\pmod p.
\]

This proves both asserted determinant congruences for every odd prime \(p\).
